newsitem.title: INDIA: Leaders scramble as India hunts for new boss.
newsitem.headline: Leaders scramble as India hunts for new boss.

text.p: India's ousted United Front coalition, preparing to form its second government in 10 months, searched on Wednesday for a leader from a growing list of contenders.
The front's challenge was to choose a man acceptable to both its regional partners and to the Congress party, a leader of the 15-party alliance said.
Congress agreed on Monday to renew vital support to ousted Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition on condition it changed leaders.

Regional Tamil leader G.K. Moopanar and Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral were joined by former finance minister Madhu Dandavate as contenders ahead of a meeting of the front's decision-making Steering Committee on Thursday.
The committee was expected to choose a new leader on Thursday. Front lawmakers would endorse the choice on Sunday.
Deve Gowda stepped down last Friday after losing a confidence vote sparked by the Congress party's withdrawal of parliamentary support on March 30.
Congress offered support to the alliance of centrists, regional parties and communists last year to oust a 12-day rule by the Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
When Congress withdrew support, it accused Deve Gowda of not containing Hindu nationalists and insisted that he must step down for Congress backing to continue.
The alliance rejected the demand and lost power on Friday. Congress changed its mind on Sunday, sparking a leadership race.
Many leaders have been mentioned in New Delhi as potential prime ministers, but most have handicaps.

Tamil Maanila Congress (TMC) leader Moopanar was a frontrunner but faces potential opposition from the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) party, which fears his rise may erode its base in Tamil Nadu state, the alliance leader said.
Jyoti Basu, leader of the Communist Party of India-Marxist (CPI-M) is acceptable to United Front allies, but last year the CPI-M had declined to join the government.
Chandrababu Naidu, leader of the Telugu Desam Party (TDP), has wide support, but has said he is not in the race as he is content to be the chief minister of his Andhra Pradesh state.
Mulayam Singh Yadav, an aggressive low-caste leader from the northern state of Uttar Pradesh, could be the Samajwadi Party's nominee, but politicians say only the communists will back him.
A choice from Deve Gowda's Janata Dal party could be acceptable to allies, but the party has internal problems. "Janata Dal is a divided house," a party leader said.
Laloo Prasad Yadav, chief minister of Bihar and the party's current president, was once considered the key man for the nation's top job, but faces the glare of a corruption scandal.
Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral is acceptable to many for his congenial manner and competence, but he has no political base.
S.R. Bommai, now India's caretaker human resource minister, is a veteran viewed as past his prime.
The affable Madhu Dandavate, currently deputy chairman of the economic Planning Commission, is not seen as being among frontrunners, but could emerge from a tight race.
The choice of a new head could be determined by a respected patron, former prime minister V.P. Singh, who is out of active politics and being treated for kidney problems.
"The next PM will be decided from Apollo Hospital," the alliance leader said.
